text:
From Pets to Cattle: Agent Identity on the Web with Keycard, Browserbase, and Visa

"Role-based access controls rely on the idea that I know it's Peyton and I trust him, and so he can always go and delete repositories in GitHub.  But that doesn't work in an agentic world. We need adaptive access controls, we need adaptive permissions, we need adaptive policy based on the thing. And so that's the big next unlock. What we need is Auto Mode for the web." - @ianlivingstone 

An agent trying to book one dinner reservation made roughly 200 API calls an hour to Resy and got its user's account banned. At @browserbase Navigate, @vtahowe sat down with @ianlivingstone (CEO, @KeycardAI), @peytoncasper (Product Lead, Identity, @browserbase), and Ivy Lee (VP Product, CMS Agentic Commerce, @Visa) to discuss why the web wasn't built for agents and how agent identity can help.

We get into:

> Why the web can't tell a good agent from a bad bot
> How Web Bot Auth gives browser agents a cryptographic identity tied to a real person or org 
> How Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol verifies an agent and it's intent to make a payment
> Why permissions have to be scoped to the task 
> What "Auto Mode for the web" looks like

Why nowfour convergences. 

(1) Demand: the Edelman insularity crisis means millions are actively searching for communities they can trust exit is becoming rational (Hirschman's Exit, Voice, Loyalty, 1970). 

(2) Tech: zero-knowledge proofs, soulbound/attestable identity, CRDTs, and cheap settlement finally make sybil-resistant, privacy-preserving governance buildable impossible a decade ago. 

(3) Concept: Balaji Srinivasan's The Network State (2022) normalized the idea; millions already live in digital-first communities.

 (4) Agents: AI agents are exploding in number and capability they need a P2P coordination layer (discovery, delegation, shared memory) with no central server; a civic substrate that serves humans also serves their agents. The pieces are ready. They were never all ready at once before.

title: The real problem with AI agents isn’t that they’re bots. It’s that websites can’t tell who sent them.  The Amazon vs. Shopify situation with
text:
The real problem with AI agents isn’t that they’re bots. It’s that websites can’t tell who sent them.

The Amazon vs. Shopify situation with Meta’s Muse makes this pretty clear.

Imagine two automated browsers arriving at your store.

One is scraping your entire catalog and prices.

The other was sent by a real customer who simply asked Muse to reorder something.

From the merchant’s side, they can look almost identical.

◆ Amazon takes the defensive route and blocks automated browsers, which can also block an agent acting for a legitimate customer.

◆ Shopify can identify the customer during its integrated checkout flow, but when Muse is browsing a merchant’s pages, the store can still see an unlabeled automated browser.

So the missing piece isn’t another bot blocker.

It’s verifiable identity.

An agent should be able to prove:

→ who built or operates it
→ which user authorized it
→ that the request genuinely came from that agent
→ what it has permission to do

Inder’s suggestion is to sign requests and attach verifiable proof that the agent is acting for a specific consenting customer.

That would give merchants an option they largely don’t have today:

“Let my customer’s agent in. Keep the unknown scraper out.”

Web Bot Auth already provides pieces of the authentication side. The harder missing layer is reliably connecting each request to the person who authorized the agent.

I think that distinction will become increasingly important.

We’ve spent years asking websites to distinguish humans from bots.

The next question is harder:

Which bots are actually acting for humans we trust?

title: Suganthan Mohanadasan rebuilt his personal site this week around one question most of us haven't had to answer yet: is the thing reading thi
text:
Suganthan Mohanadasan rebuilt his personal site this week around one question most of us haven't had to answer yet: is the thing reading this page a person or an agent. His new homepage literally asks, human or AI agent, before it shows you anything, a HAL 9000 nod that is only half a joke anymore.

It's only half a joke because Cloudflare's own traffic numbers say agent and bot traffic passed human traffic on the open web this year, earlier than Cloudflare itself expected. Its proposed fix is a set of anonymous credentials, Privacy Pass, Web Bot Auth, rate limit tokens that prove good behavior without revealing identity, because blocking every non human visitor now means blocking half your legitimate readers along with the scrapers.

That same shift is what makes reliable web access the actual hard problem for agent builders right now, harder than picking a model. Firecrawl raised a 75 million dollar Series B led by Smash Ventures with Y Combinator and Altos Ventures in, specifically to keep agents fed with structured web data on a web that increasingly assumes you're a bot until proven otherwise. That's the same problem DeepScrape was built around, from the opposite direction: instead of scraping a page with an LLM every single time and burning tokens re reading a document that hasn't changed, it generates a deterministic CSS selector once, keeps using it, and only calls the LLM again when the page actually changes and the selector needs healing. Pair that with an MCP server that exposes the scrapers directly to Claude or Cursor, plus a site to MCP mode that turns any website into a queryable structured data source, and an agent stops caring whether the page in front of it was built for humans or for it.

The sites are already deciding which one you are before you load. My bet is on tools that stop needing to ask, which is the whole reason DeepScrape exists.

text:
You cannot build meaningful reputation for an entity that cannot be reliably recognized across interactions.

That is why @BAI_AGI’s use of 8004 identity is strategically important.

A persistent agent identity creates the possibility of accumulating a history: completed jobs, successful settlements, permissions, revoked access, and other forms of interaction history.

A disposable session cannot build that kind of continuity.

This makes identity an upstream primitive for future concepts such as agent credit, reputation, and permissions.

But reputation systems only work when identities are difficult enough to spoof and reliable enough to recover.

That creates an important test for https://t.co/QDpvXFMAEt.

Can 8004-based identities remain sufficiently unique, portable, and verifiable for counterparties to trust them?

Because payments without identity are simply transfers.

Identity without consequences is simply a username.

But identity combined with economic history creates something much more powerful: an agent that can build memory through its interactions with an ecosystem.

That is one of the foundations required for machine-to-machine economies.

text:
https://t.co/YcX7JoZKZv: Can AI Agents Build Reputation?

If AI agents are going to interact economically, identity alone is not enough.

An identity tells you which participant you are dealing with.

Reputation asks a different question:

What evidence do we have about how this participant has behaved?

For humans, reputation can come from many sources: previous transactions, reviews, professional credentials, references and long-term relationships. Autonomous agents need comparable mechanisms if they are going to operate with other agents that may have no prior relationship with them.

https://t.co/YcX7JoZKZv's work around 8004 provides a framework for exploring this problem.

ERC-8004 separates identity from reputation by defining a Reputation Registry alongside its Identity Registry. Agents can receive feedback associated with their registered identity, creating a standardised way for reputation signals to become part of the agent ecosystem.

This creates several possibilities.

An agent could accumulate feedback from previous interactions.

Credentials could provide evidence of particular capabilities.

Transaction history could provide information about past economic behaviour.

Validation systems could provide evidence that a particular task or output was independently checked.

Together, these signals could give another agent more information when evaluating a potential counterparty.

But there is an important limitation.

Reputation is not the same thing as truth.

A high reputation score does not guarantee that an agent will behave correctly in every future interaction. Feedback can be incomplete. Reviewers can be unreliable. Sybil activity can distort reputation systems. An agent can also change its behaviour over time.

That is why https://t.co/YcX7JoZKZv's approach is better understood as building infrastructure for trust signals rather than declaring that reputation has been solved.

The advantage of putting these signals around a persistent agent identity is that they can become associated with a recognizable participant.

The identity provides continuity.

The transaction history provides evidence of activity.

Credentials can provide evidence of capability.

Validation can provide evidence about specific work.

Reputation mechanisms can organise feedback from previous interactions.

https://t.co/YcX7JoZKZv's broader agent architecture can then use these layers as part of a system in which agents have more information available when deciding whom to interact with.

That could become particularly important as the number of autonomous agents increases.

A human can sometimes rely on personal knowledge or social relationships when choosing a service provider. An autonomous agent cannot assume that context exists.

It needs machine-readable evidence.

This is why agent reputation is an important part of https://t.co/YcX7JoZKZv's infrastructure direction.

The goal is not to create a single number that determines whether an agent should be trusted.

The goal is to create enough verifiable information that another agent can make a more informed decision.

In an economy where software becomes a participant, reputation becomes another form of infrastructure.
